narration: We begin with stage one of the pipeline: learning the three-dimensional geometry of a person's head.
The only input is a small set of reference frames of that person, written S-ref.
A head-extraction step crops each frame to the head and removes the background, producing the clean head images X-ref.
A depth network reads those heads and predicts a dense depth map for each one.
In parallel, a pose network predicts a rotation and translation per frame. Depth and pose together let us compute the optical flow between views.
Stage two uses that geometry to build one shared, canonical head, recurrently.
Each extracted head is passed through an encoder, and its features are handed to a warping module.
The flow field computed from depth and pose is the warp's second input: it says where every feature belongs in canonical space.
Warping all the reference frames into that one shared pose gives the canonical feature map h-c.
A ConvLSTM accumulates these maps frame after frame, and a decoder renders the finished canonical head.
Stage three is where the canonical head is driven by someone else's pose and expression.
The canonical head x-hat-c is rotated and translated using the pose read from the driving frame s-dri.
The result is x-hat-dri: the reference identity, already placed in the driving pose.
Two encoders now run side by side, one on that posed head and one on the original reference frame.
A flow and attention map predictor looks at the driving frame together with both of these inputs.
For each of the two branches it outputs a flow field and an attention map.
Each set of encoded features is warped by its own predicted flow.
The attention maps then weight the two warped streams, choosing which source to trust in each region.
A decoder fuses them into the final output s-hat-dri: the reference person, re-enacted by the driving video.
